title: Two Snails and a Race
summary: Cala and Lito race to the rosebush. Halfway there they find a fallen nest, and they have to decide what matters more.

scenes.text:
In a garden full of flowers lived two snails: Cala and Lito.

Cala's shell was every colour, like a sweet. Lito's was pink, and he always kept it very clean.

Lito loved winning. Winning at who woke up first. Winning at who ate the biggest leaf. Winning at everything.

"I challenge you to a race," he said to Cala one morning. "To the rosebush."

The rosebush was on the other side of the garden. For a snail, that is very, very far.

"All right," said Cala. "But no pushing."

An orange butterfly offered to be the judge. She perched on the starting line and shouted:

"Go!"

The slowest race in the world had begun.

Lito stretched out his neck and pushed forward with all his might. Behind him he left a shiny thread, straight as a ruler.

Cala went more slowly. She stopped to smell a flower. She said hello to an ant. Her silver thread made curves, and curls, and squiggles.

"I'm winning!" shouted Lito, without even turning his head.

By midday, Lito had reached the trunk of the big tree, halfway there.

And there, in the middle of the path, was a nest.

It had fallen from the branches in the night wind. Inside, on a mattress of fluff, were four blue eggs.

Lito looked at the nest. He looked at the rosebush, far away. And he kept going.

"It's none of my business," he muttered. "I'm in a race."

A good while later, Cala arrived, slowly, with her curly thread behind her.

She saw the nest and stopped dead.

"Poor little things," she said. "If they stay here on the ground, they'll get cold. And their mother won't find them."

Cala settled down next to the eggs, to keep them company. And she stayed there, even though the race went on.

Lito could see the rosebush very close now. A few more little steps and he would win.

But he glanced behind him.

Far away, by the tree, a colourful shell wasn't moving. Cala had stayed there on her own, looking after the nest.

Lito thought about winning. He thought about the eggs. He thought about Cala.

And he turned around.

It took him the whole afternoon to return. When he arrived he was worn out, and the sun was already going down.

"What about the race?" Cala asked.

"Forget the race," said Lito. "How do we find their mother?"

The two snails looked up. High above, among the branches, a mother bird was flying to and fro, searching and searching for her nest.

But from so high up, the nest was just one more little speck on the ground.

"Here! Down here!" they shouted with all their strength.

But a snail's voice is smaller than a whisper.

Then Cala looked at her shiny thread. And she had an idea.

"She can't hear us," she said. "But she can see us."

The two of them began to crawl beside the nest. Lito made the straight lines, the way he knew how. Cala made the curves. Over and over, until there on the ground was drawn an enormous silver arrow, pointing at the nest.

At that moment, the last ray of sun fell across the path.

And the arrow began to glow.

It shone like a river of silver. From high above, the mother bird saw it. And she swooped down, beating her wings.

There was her nest, with all four eggs, whole and warm.

That night, she carried it back up to the safest branch in the tree.

And the next morning, she came down to fetch two snails. She lifted them onto her back, very carefully, and flew them over the whole garden.

All the way to the rosebush.

They both arrived at exactly the same time. And the butterfly, who had seen everything, said it was the loveliest race she had ever judged.
